title: Transactions & ACID
subtitle: All or nothing — and the dial most engineers don't know they're turning
objectives: Explain atomicity and why a half-finished transfer is worse than none
Define each letter of ACID, and why C is the odd one out
Choose an isolation level knowingly, and recognize the anomalies each one allows
Handle deadlocks, keep transactions short, and know where atomicity stops

exercises.prompt: Transfer $100: subtract from account A, then add to account B. The server crashes between the two steps. What happened?
choices: $100 vanished — it left A and never arrived at B
exercises.why: Two writes that must both happen or neither. Crash in the middle and you've destroyed money — with no error, and no way for either account to know.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the canonical example for a reason: it's the clearest case where 'half done' is strictly worse than 'not done at all.' A failed transfer is an inconvenience. A half transfer is a corrupted ledger, and nobody can tell by looking at it.

exercises.prompt: A ______ groups multiple operations so they all succeed together or all fail together.
exercises.why: A transaction turns many operations into one indivisible unit — the database's answer to 'half done.'

exercises.prompt: What does COMMIT actually mean?
choices: Apply every change in the transaction — all of them, together
Write to a log file for later
exercises.why: COMMIT applies your whole transaction as one unit. ROLLBACK is the opposite: discard everything since BEGIN, as though it never happened.
exercises.goDeeper: The load-bearing word is 'together': either the whole transaction takes effect, or none of it does — there is no outcome in which half of it stuck. That is all atomicity claims, and it's worth holding it exactly that narrowly. Note it's a claim about the OUTCOME, not about any moment along the way: mid-transaction, some of your writes have obviously happened and some haven't — that's just executing. The other ACID letters make their own, quite different promises, and quietly blurring them into atomicity is the most common way people misread what a transaction actually guarantees. Lesson 2 pulls them apart one at a time.

exercises.prompt: You're 5 of 10 writes into a transaction when it hits an error and rolls back. What happens to those 5 writes?
choices: All 5 are undone: the database rewinds to the state at BEGIN
Only the most recent one is undone
The database pauses and asks you what to do
exercises.why: That's atomicity: the transaction is indivisible, so a failure anywhere undoes everything since BEGIN. You can never be left with a half-finished transfer sitting in the data.
exercises.goDeeper: Be careful with a related-but-different question: could OTHER transactions have seen those 5 writes before you committed? That is NOT atomicity — it's isolation, and the answer depends on the isolation level you're running (at Read Uncommitted they genuinely could — a 'dirty read'). Atomicity is only about whether you can be left half-done. Lesson 3 takes isolation apart properly.

exercises.prompt: Order the life of a transaction.
steps: All the changes take effect together
exercises.why: Open it, do the work, commit — and only at COMMIT do all the changes take effect, as one unit. Anything before that point can still be undone.
exercises.goDeeper: If anything fails between BEGIN and COMMIT — an error, a crash, a ROLLBACK — the database rewinds to the state at BEGIN. That rewind is exactly what the write-ahead log from unit 6 makes possible.

exercises.prompt: Why is a transaction the right tool for a bank transfer, but overkill for logging one analytics event?
choices: A transfer has an invariant spanning two rows that must never break; a lone analytics insert has nothing to be atomic with
Transactions are always the right tool
exercises.why: Atomicity matters when several changes must hold together. A single independent insert is already all-or-nothing by itself — wrapping it in a transaction buys you nothing.
exercises.goDeeper: Good instinct to build: reach for a transaction when there's an invariant across multiple writes. The question is never 'is this important data?' — it's 'is there a rule that would break if only some of this landed?'

exercises.prompt: Match each letter of ACID to what it promises.

pairs.right: Your declared rules are never violated
Concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other
Committed means it survives a crash

exercises.why: Four promises: indivisible, rule-abiding, non-interfering, and permanent.
exercises.goDeeper: They're not equally interesting, which the acronym hides. Two of them are essentially on/off, one is barely the database's doing, and one is a dial you're probably turning without realising. The rest of this lesson sorts out which is which.

exercises.prompt: Durability: you commit, and a microsecond later the power dies. Your data?
choices: Lost — it was still in memory
There — commit meant it was durably recorded before the database answered you
Recovered only if you had a backup
exercises.why: That's the D, and it's the promise you met in unit 6: the write-ahead log is forced to disk before COMMIT returns.
exercises.goDeeper: Which is why COMMIT isn't instant — it's waiting on physics. Every 'why are my writes slow?' question eventually arrives at this: you asked for a guarantee that requires the disk to confirm.

exercises.prompt: Which letter of ACID is really about YOUR rules rather than the database's own machinery?
choices: Consistency — it just means the constraints you declared (unique, foreign keys, checks) hold before and after
exercises.why: A, I, and D are properties the engine provides. C only says: the database won't let you violate the constraints you defined. If you declared no constraints, C promises approximately nothing.
exercises.goDeeper: Plenty of practitioners argue the C is a bit of a cheat — it's really 'the database enforces your declared invariants,' which is just... constraints. The genuinely hard letters are A, I, and D. And watch out: the C in CAP means something completely different, a collision of names that has confused engineers for twenty years.

exercises.prompt: Which ACID property do you actually have to make decisions about?
choices: Atomicity — you configure how atomic it is
Isolation — it's a dial with several settings, each trading correctness for speed
Consistency — you tune it per query
exercises.why: Atomicity and durability are essentially on or off — you get them. Isolation is a spectrum you configure, and the setting decides which concurrency bugs remain possible.
exercises.goDeeper: Here's the uncomfortable part: most engineers cannot tell you what isolation level their production database runs at. They're relying on guarantees they've never looked up — and the defaults are not the strongest ones. That's the next lesson.

exercises.prompt: Which of these statements are TRUE? Select all.
choices: Isolation is a single fixed guarantee every database provides identically
The C in ACID means something different from the C in CAP
exercises.why: Isolation is the odd one — it's configurable, and databases differ in both their defaults and what their level names actually mean.
exercises.goDeeper: That last point is a genuine trap: two databases can both say 'Repeatable Read' and give you materially different guarantees. The label is not the specification.

exercises.prompt: A colleague says 'we use Postgres, so we're ACID — concurrency bugs are impossible.' What's wrong?
choices: ACID doesn't mean 'maximum isolation.' The default level still permits real anomalies; you have to opt into stronger guarantees
exercises.why: 'ACID compliant' is not a force field. The I in ACID is whatever level you're running — and the default is not serializable.
exercises.goDeeper: This misconception causes real bugs. Teams assume the database is protecting an invariant it was never asked to protect, then find corrupted data months later with no error in any log. Concurrency bugs don't crash — they quietly lie.

exercises.prompt: Why don't databases just always use the strictest isolation?
choices: Stricter isolation costs performance — more locking or coordination and more aborted transactions — so you get to choose
exercises.why: Isolation is bought with throughput. The stricter you go, the more the database must coordinate or abort, so it lets you pick your point on the curve.
exercises.goDeeper: And the defaults are NOT the strictest. Postgres defaults to Read Committed; MySQL's InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read. Neither is serializable. So unless you changed it deliberately, you are running with known anomalies permitted — right now, in production.

exercises.prompt: Match each concurrency anomaly to what goes wrong.

pairs.right: You read data another transaction hasn't committed
You read the same row twice and get different values
You re-run a range query and new rows appear
Two read-modify-writes; one is silently overwritten

exercises.why: Each isolation level is defined by which of these it forbids. Knowing the anomalies is how you read the levels.
exercises.goDeeper: You already met lost update in unit 6 — the counter that went from 10 to 11 instead of 12. It wasn't a database bug; it was an isolation level doing exactly what it promised, which was less than you assumed.

exercises.prompt: Order the isolation levels from weakest to strongest.
exercises.why: Each rung forbids more anomalies and costs more coordination. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads; Read Committed stops them; Repeatable Read stops non-repeatable reads; Serializable stops everything.
exercises.goDeeper: Read Uncommitted is almost never worth using — you get dirty reads for a performance win that modern engines barely deliver. The real decision in practice is between Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable.

exercises.prompt: What does Serializable actually guarantee?
choices: Transactions literally run one at a time, so it's very slow
The RESULT is as if they'd run one at a time in some order — even though they ran concurrently
exercises.why: It's a promise about the outcome, not the schedule. The database may run everything concurrently, as long as the final state matches SOME serial order.
exercises.goDeeper: That 'as if' does enormous work. The engine may let transactions run in parallel and then ABORT one when it spots a conflict that couldn't have arisen serially. Which means under Serializable your transaction can fail through no fault of its own — and your code must be ready to retry. Correctness didn't become free; it moved into your error handling.

exercises.prompt: Two doctors are on call. Each opens a transaction, checks 'is at least one OTHER doctor on call?', sees yes, and books themselves off. Both commit. Now nobody is on call — though each transaction was individually valid. What is this?
choices: Write skew — they read overlapping data but wrote to different rows, so nothing conflicted
exercises.why: No two transactions touched the same row, so most isolation levels see no conflict at all. Yet together they broke an invariant that neither broke alone.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the anomaly that snapshot isolation — which is what Postgres's 'Repeatable Read' actually is — still permits, and that Serializable prevents. It's subtle precisely BECAUSE nothing overlapped: the bug lives in a rule spanning rows, not in any single row. If your correctness depends on an invariant across multiple rows, Read Committed and Repeatable Read will not save you.

exercises.prompt: Your correctness depends on an invariant spanning multiple rows that must never break. What do you do?
choices: Use Serializable and handle retries, take an explicit lock, or restructure so the invariant lives in a single row
exercises.why: Three real options: pay for Serializable (and be ready to retry), lock explicitly so conflicts are visible, or reshape the data so the rule is enforceable in one place.
exercises.goDeeper: That third option is underrated. If the invariant can be expressed as a single row — a counter, a constraint, a unique key — the database can enforce it cheaply and unconditionally. Often the best fix for a hard concurrency problem is a better data model, not a stronger isolation level.

exercises.prompt: Transaction 1 locks row A and then wants row B. Transaction 2 locks row B and then wants row A. What happens?
choices: Deadlock — the database detects the cycle, kills one, and that one gets an error and must retry
exercises.why: Each holds what the other needs. Real databases detect the cycle and abort a victim rather than hanging forever — so one transaction gets an error out of nowhere.
exercises.goDeeper: The classic prevention is to always acquire locks in a consistent order — e.g. always lock the lower account id first, so a cycle can't form. Deadlocks aren't a database defect; they're an emergent property of concurrent code, and your app must be prepared to retry.

exercises.prompt: You open a transaction and hold it for 10 minutes while calling an external payment API inside it. What's the damage?
choices: You hold locks the whole time, block other transactions, and force the database to retain old row versions — bloating storage and slowing everything
exercises.why: A held transaction holds locks and pins old versions of rows. Everyone who needs those rows queues behind you — for as long as a third party takes to answer.
exercises.goDeeper: The rule: never do network I/O inside a transaction. This is one of the most common real production outages there is — the slow API call holds locks, waiting transactions pile up (unit 4's queueing), the connection pool exhausts, and a payments hiccup becomes a total site outage. Do the I/O first, then open a short transaction to record the result.

exercises.prompt: Match each concurrency strategy to what it is.

pairs.right: Lock up front — assume conflict is likely
Proceed, detect conflict at commit, retry
How optimistic concurrency spots a conflict
Two transactions each holding what the other wants

exercises.why: Two philosophies: prevent conflicts by excluding others, or allow them and detect collisions at the end.
exercises.goDeeper: Optimistic concurrency is usually a version column: read version 7, write only if it's still 7. If someone else got there first it's now 8, your update matches nothing, and you retry. It's just compare-and-set, applied to a row.

exercises.prompt: Your workload has rare conflicts — users almost never edit the same row simultaneously. Which strategy usually wins?
choices: Optimistic concurrency — conflicts are rare, so occasionally retrying beats making everyone wait
exercises.why: If collisions are rare, locking everyone up front taxes the 99% of transactions that would never have conflicted. Let them run and pay only when you actually collide.
exercises.goDeeper: And the inverse matters just as much: under HIGH contention, optimistic degenerates — everyone retries, collides again, and you burn capacity making no progress. Pessimistic is calmer there. Choose from how often you actually collide, not from which sounds more sophisticated.

exercises.prompt: You must charge a credit card (an external service) AND create an order (your database) atomically. Can a database transaction do this?
choices: No — a database transaction only covers its own database; the card charge is a separate system that knows nothing about your COMMIT or ROLLBACK
exercises.why: Atomicity stops at the database boundary. Your ROLLBACK can rewind your rows — it cannot un-charge someone's card.
exercises.goDeeper: This is where people get badly burned, because the code LOOKS atomic. The real patterns are: two-phase commit (a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, then commit — correct, but slow, and it blocks if the coordinator dies mid-flight), or a saga (do the steps, and if a later one fails, run compensating actions — issue a refund). Most modern systems choose sagas plus idempotency (unit 2) over 2PC.

exercises.prompt: Microservices: an order service and a payment service, each with its own database. Slide toward your approach for keeping them consistent.
exercises.why: Across services, 2PC's blocking behaviour and coordinator failure modes are usually worse than the complexity of writing compensating actions. Most real distributed systems choose sagas.
exercises.goDeeper: But be honest about what you just gave up: there's now a window where the payment succeeded and the order doesn't exist yet. You accepted a temporarily inconsistent state plus a compensation path — because the alternative, a distributed lock spanning services, is worse. That acceptance is the road to eventual consistency, and it's where Tier 3 begins.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of transactions?
choices: Always use Serializable and never think about it again
A transaction buys atomicity and a chosen isolation level within ONE database — so know your level, keep transactions short, and remember the guarantee stops at the database boundary
Transactions are legacy; use eventual consistency everywhere
exercises.why: Powerful, bounded, and configurable. The power is real; the boundary and the dial are what people forget.
exercises.goDeeper: Three things most engineers get wrong, in order of damage: (1) they don't know their isolation level, (2) they hold transactions open across network calls, (3) they assume atomicity extends across services. Fix those three and you're ahead of most working engineers — and you're ready for what happens when the copies can't talk to each other.
